    <title>Calsequestrin localization at RyR2 clusters enables calcium wave propagation in ventricular myocytes</title>
    <link rel="alternate" href="https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014449" title="Calsequestrin localization at RyR2 clusters enables calcium wave propagation in ventricular myocytes" />
    <link rel="related" type="application/pdf" href="https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article/asset?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014449.PDF" title="(PDF) Calsequestrin localization at RyR2 clusters enables calcium wave propagation in ventricular myocytes" />

    <author>
      <name>David Conesa</name>
    </author>
    <author>
      <name>Blas Echebarria</name>
    </author>
    <author>
      <name>Leif Hove-Madsen</name>
    </author>
    <author>
      <name>Yohannes Shiferaw</name>
    </author>
    <author>
      <name>Enrique Alvarez-Lacalle</name>
    </author>
    <id>10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014449</id>
    <updated>2026-10-26T14:00:00Z</updated>
    <published>2026-10-26T14:00:00Z</published>
    <content type="html"><p>by David Conesa, Blas Echebarria, Leif Hove-Madsen, Yohannes Shiferaw, Enrique Alvarez-Lacalle</p>

Intracellular calcium waves in cardiac myocytes propagate through a fire-diffuse-fire mechanism in which calcium released from one RyR2 cluster diffuses to neighboring clusters and triggers their activation. Yet propagation faces a fundamental physical difficulty: the calcium signal must cross distances of 1–2 <i>μ</i>m between Z-planes while being attenuated by cytosolic buffering and diffusion, and at the same time the release site depletes its local sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium store. How waves propagate efficiently despite these constraints has remained unclear. We developed a three-dimensional computational model of mouse ventricular myocytes at submicrometer resolution to address this question. Our central finding is that co-localization of calsequestrin2 (CASQ2) with RyR2 clusters is required for robust wave propagation. In a physiological model, where CASQ2 is concentrated at release sites as observed experimentally, calcium waves propagate reliably across the cell with velocities that match the experimental range. In contrast, when CASQ2 is distributed uniformly throughout the sarcoplasmic reticulum, keeping total CASQ2 unchanged, the wavefront stalls. These results identify CASQ2–RyR2 co-localization as a key structural requirement for effective calcium wave propagation in ventricular myocytes.</content>

    <title>An integrative computational approach for obstacle avoidance during action selection</title>
    <link rel="alternate" href="https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1013756" title="An integrative computational approach for obstacle avoidance during action selection" />
    <link rel="related" type="application/pdf" href="https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article/asset?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1013756.PDF" title="(PDF) An integrative computational approach for obstacle avoidance during action selection" />
    <link rel="related" type="text/xml" href="https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article/asset?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1013756.XML" title="(XML) An integrative computational approach for obstacle avoidance during action selection" />
    <author>
      <name>Shan Zhong</name>
    </author>
    <author>
      <name>Nader Pouratian</name>
    </author>
    <author>
      <name>Paul Schrater</name>
    </author>
    <author>
      <name>Vassilios Christopoulos</name>
    </author>
    <id>10.1371/journal.pcbi.1013756</id>
    <updated>2026-10-26T14:00:00Z</updated>
    <published>2026-10-26T14:00:00Z</published>
    <content type="html"><p>by Shan Zhong, Nader Pouratian, Paul Schrater, Vassilios Christopoulos</p>

Action selection in cluttered environments, where individuals must simultaneously pursue goals and avoid obstacles, presents a significant challenge for the brain. To understand the underlying mechanisms of action selection in such contexts, we propose a computational model that extends stochastic optimal control theory through a novel framework for obstacle avoidance. The model decomposes action selection into a weighted combination of individual control policies, each generated for either target approach or obstacle avoidance. By integrating value information from goals, obstacles, and actions into a unified measure of “relative desirability”, the model dynamically determines the contribution of each policy to the overall action selection process. We evaluated the framework using simulated target-reaching tasks in cluttered environments based on previous human studies. The results showed that the model qualitatively captures key features of human motor behavior, including the influence of obstacle properties on movement trajectories and the transient tendency to initiate movements toward obstacles before avoidance.This work offers new insights into the dynamic interaction between approach and avoidance behaviors, providing a basis for future studies of action selection in more complex and naturalistic settings.</content>

    <title>A computational framework for modeling fluid and solid stressesin porous tissues with application to the trabeculated embryonic heart</title>
    <link rel="alternate" href="https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014896" title="A computational framework for modeling fluid and solid stressesin porous tissues with application to the trabeculated embryonic heart" />
    <link rel="related" type="application/pdf" href="https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article/asset?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014896.PDF" title="(PDF) A computational framework for modeling fluid and solid stressesin porous tissues with application to the trabeculated embryonic heart" />
    <link rel="related" type="text/xml" href="https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article/asset?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014896.XML" title="(XML) A computational framework for modeling fluid and solid stressesin porous tissues with application to the trabeculated embryonic heart" />
    <author>
      <name>Christine Miller Buffinton</name>
    </author>
    <author>
      <name>James W. Baish</name>
    </author>
    <id>10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014896</id>
    <updated>2026-10-23T14:00:00Z</updated>
    <published>2026-10-23T14:00:00Z</published>
    <content type="html"><p>by Christine Miller Buffinton, James W. Baish</p>

This study provides a framework for efficient solutions of computational fluid-solid interaction models of porous tissue, with a focus on blood flow through the developing heart wall in the critical chamber and valve formation stages, when trabeculation fills much of the ventricles. This porous, trabeculated tissue is the site of complex mechanotransduction processes, but accurately estimating solid and fluid stresses within such intricate geometries is difficult. We addressed this with three levels of modeling and verification. Images of E12.5 mouse ventricles were first obtained through confocal microscopy and 3D reconstruction. These guided creation of explicit pore-scale finite element simulations with fluid-solid interaction. Idealized and image-derived unit cells were analyzed to determine hydraulic permeability. Next, a multi-pore representation of the ventricular wall was solved with full fluid and solid equations. A continuum model based on Brinkman equations then replaced the explicit pore structure, and sensitivity to permeability was evaluated in terms of fluid flow in the open channel and porous region. Permeabilities obtained from unit cell simulations followed trends from Kozeny-Carman solid-pore and fiber theory for the rigid case, while simulations for hyperelastic unit-cell material quantified the effects of tissue elasticity. Comparison of continuum and explicit model results showed the Brinkman equation, which incorporates the diffusion of shear stress from flow in the free fluid into the porous media, but not explicitly inertial effects, could significantly improve the accuracy of continuum models compared to Darcy's law. A 3D model of blood flow through the ventricles of the developing mouse heart demonstrated the application of the technique to more realistic geometry, showed locations of peak solid and shear stress, and produced physiologically reasonable flow. Furthermore, we developed methodologies to estimate local wall shear and solid stress from continuum-based calculations. This approach can enable efficient, whole-organ parametric analyses of fluid flow, circumventing the need for computationally expensive explicit pore modeling.</content>

    <title>Visuomotor coordination on the road: Low-dimensional representations reveal adaptive, context-dependent reductions in the dimensionality of natural driving behavior</title>
    <link rel="alternate" href="https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014056" title="Visuomotor coordination on the road: Low-dimensional representations reveal adaptive, context-dependent reductions in the dimensionality of natural driving behavior" />
    <link rel="related" type="application/pdf" href="https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article/asset?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014056.PDF" title="(PDF) Visuomotor coordination on the road: Low-dimensional representations reveal adaptive, context-dependent reductions in the dimensionality of natural driving behavior" />
    <link rel="related" type="text/xml" href="https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article/asset?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014056.XML" title="(XML) Visuomotor coordination on the road: Low-dimensional representations reveal adaptive, context-dependent reductions in the dimensionality of natural driving behavior" />
    <author>
      <name>John Madrid-Carvajal</name>
    </author>
    <author>
      <name>Shadi Derakhshan</name>
    </author>
    <author>
      <name>Peter König</name>
    </author>
    <id>10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014056</id>
    <updated>2026-10-23T14:00:00Z</updated>
    <published>2026-10-23T14:00:00Z</published>
    <content type="html"><p>by John Madrid-Carvajal, Shadi Derakhshan, Peter König</p>

The brain’s ability to transform complex, high-dimensional sensory and motor inputs into coordinated, goal-directed behavior remains a central challenge in neuroscience research. Current research suggests that behavior is generated through patterns within a low-dimensional structure. What visuomotor patterns underlie complex, unconstrained behaviors such as driving, and how stereotypical they are, remain poorly understood. Driving involves complex perception-action interactions, which we hypothesize are specific to the driver’s role and adapt to task demands. Here, we unfold these dynamics using an immersive virtual drive that recreates ten hazardous on-road events. We collected eye, head, and vehicle movements from participants assigned to either a manual or an automated driving condition. From the behavioral movements of 284 drivers, we constructed a common time-resolved behavioral state space based on collective variance, computed via principal component analysis across participants. The obtained low-dimensional representation thus captures generalized visuomotor coordination strategies. We then characterized the evolving low-dimensional structure with cosine similarity and various measures of effective dimensionality. We tested whether leading components contained condition-specific information using discriminant analysis. Throughout the entire drive, few components accounted for most of the variance in behavior, and effective dimensionality decreased reliably around critical events, indicating tighter coordination between perceptual and motor variables. During periods of low effective dimensionality, the contributions of eye, head, steering, and vehicle heading reorganized toward leading dimensions in a task-dependent manner. Across events, between-subject similarity was partially stable and stronger among manual drivers. This reorganization also made behaviors more distinct across driving conditions, enabling better classification of driving modes using only the first two components. These results show that naturalistic driving is supported by shared low-dimensional visuomotor coordination strategies that are flexibly reshaped by contextual demands, and provide a principled behavioral framework for linking neural manifolds, human driver models, and the design of adaptive automated vehicles.</content>

    <title>Cell-type dependence of effects from transcranial electric brain stimulation</title>
    <link rel="alternate" href="https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014895" title="Cell-type dependence of effects from transcranial electric brain stimulation" />
    <link rel="related" type="application/pdf" href="https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article/asset?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014895.PDF" title="(PDF) Cell-type dependence of effects from transcranial electric brain stimulation" />
    <link rel="related" type="text/xml" href="https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article/asset?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014895.XML" title="(XML) Cell-type dependence of effects from transcranial electric brain stimulation" />
    <author>
      <name>Susanne Dahle</name>
    </author>
    <author>
      <name>Gaute T. Einevoll</name>
    </author>
    <author>
      <name>Torbjørn V. Ness</name>
    </author>
    <id>10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014895</id>
    <updated>2026-10-22T14:00:00Z</updated>
    <published>2026-10-22T14:00:00Z</published>
    <content type="html"><p>by Susanne Dahle, Gaute T. Einevoll, Torbjørn V. Ness</p>

There is an urgent need for better treatment options for many neurological conditions, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, depression, and epilepsy. Transcranial electrical stimulation (tES) is a non-invasive, safe, inexpensive, and promising method that could address some of this unmet need. The therapeutic value of tES has been well demonstrated, but the effect is highly variable. To enable tES to reach its full potential requires a better understanding of how tES modulates neural activity so that tES treatments can be tailored to specific neurological conditions and individual patients. The neural response to tES is, however, highly complex, and the parameter space involved in optimizing tES treatments is daunting. This has made it difficult to obtain general insights into how tES modulates neural activity, and a central challenge lies in the cell-type-specific and frequency-dependent nature of these responses. In this study, we investigated cell-type-specific neuronal responses to tES over a broad frequency range, using a large database of biophysically detailed neuron models. We found that pyramidal cells respond strongly to low-frequency tES, but their responses drop sharply with frequency. In contrast, inhibitory neurons show a smaller reduction and, on average, become more responsive than pyramidal cells above ~60 Hz. By leveraging a reciprocity theorem we demonstrated that the effect of tES on a given cell-type is proportional to the frequency-dependent current-dipole moment that determines the EEG-signal contribution of this cell-type. We further identified the dendritic asymmetry as key in determining tES responses across the frequency spectrum. Counterintuitively, we also found that while total cell length increases tES sensitivity at low frequencies, it can have the opposite effect at high frequencies. Furthermore, we derived an analytical formula for idealized neuron models which can approximately predict the tES sensitivity of different cell types at any given frequency. By characterizing the role of morphology and stimulation frequency in determining tES responses of single cells, this is an important step towards a better understanding of tES at the fundamental level. These results also provide an efficient and accurate method for characterizing and comparing the tES responses of different neural populations across the frequency spectrum, which facilitates optimizing tES for cell-type specific targeting.</content>

    <title>The evolutionary accessibility of cultural fitness landscapes</title>
    <link rel="alternate" href="https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014830" title="The evolutionary accessibility of cultural fitness landscapes" />
    <link rel="related" type="application/pdf" href="https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article/asset?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014830.PDF" title="(PDF) The evolutionary accessibility of cultural fitness landscapes" />
    <link rel="related" type="text/xml" href="https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article/asset?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014830.XML" title="(XML) The evolutionary accessibility of cultural fitness landscapes" />
    <author>
      <name>Laurel Fogarty</name>
    </author>
    <author>
      <name>Rebecca B. Hoyle</name>
    </author>
    <id>10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014830</id>
    <updated>2026-10-22T14:00:00Z</updated>
    <published>2026-10-22T14:00:00Z</published>
    <content type="html"><p>by Laurel Fogarty, Rebecca B. Hoyle</p>

Many human cultural and technological traits have a complex and peculiar structure. They are often characterized by multiple closely interacting parts that can form modules, and change as a result of innovation, collaboration, and social learning. A full understanding of the ways in which such cultural traits evolve requires a model that accounts for the close epistatic interaction of the constituent parts, and for the uniquely cultural processes that act on them. Here, we generalize the concept of ‘adaptive landscapes’, where populations search a landscape for optimal combinations of components. This generalization accounts for epistatic interactions, and includes processes such as modularization, communication, and collaboration, that are not features of genetic systems but may be quite common features of cultural systems. We show that modularization in combination with collaborative communication of search results is more successful, but sometimes more costly, than searching a full adaptive landscape. However, in many of the circumstances under which technology evolves, a full search of many thousands of possible modules may not be feasible since time, financial, energetic, and environmental constraints are likely to be strong. Under these conditions, our models suggest that there is a critical value for the number of modules to search below which the global optimum is more likely to be reached by searching the full landscape. The value of this threshold depends on the complexity of the technology. Overall, we suggest that analysis of cultural fitness landscapes is likely to be a fruitful avenue for research into technological change especially when combined with elements of human learning and interaction known to be important features of cultural evolution.</content>

    <title>Proton transport drives allosteric conformational changes in the MmpL3 transporter</title>
    <link rel="alternate" href="https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014880" title="Proton transport drives allosteric conformational changes in the MmpL3 transporter" />
    <link rel="related" type="application/pdf" href="https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article/asset?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014880.PDF" title="(PDF) Proton transport drives allosteric conformational changes in the MmpL3 transporter" />

      <name>E. Jeffrey North</name>
    </author>
    <author>
      <name>Helen I. Zgurskaya</name>
    </author>
    <author>
      <name>Mary Jackson</name>
    </author>

      <name>James C. Gumbart</name>
    </author>

    <updated>2026-10-21T14:00:00Z</updated>
    <published>2026-10-21T14:00:00Z</published>
    <content type="html"><p>by Lixinhao Yang, E. Jeffrey North, Helen I. Zgurskaya, Mary Jackson, James C. Gumbart</p>

Tuberculosis (TB), caused by <i>Mycobacterium tuberculosis</i> (<i>Mtb</i>), remains a global health crisis, further complicated by increasing drug resistance. The mycobacterial membrane protein MmpL3, which is essential for transporting cell wall precursors such as trehalose monomycolate (TMM), is a promising therapeutic target. However, the mechanistic link between proton-driven dynamics and substrate transport in MmpL3 is not fully understood. In this study, we use molecular dynamics simulations to investigate how protonation of conserved Asp-Tyr dyads (Asp256-Tyr646 and Asp645-Tyr257) in <i>Mycobacterium smegmatis</i> (<i>Msmg</i>) MmpL3 regulates conformational changes and TMM binding. Protonation at Asp256 induces an open dyad conformation, increases local water accessibility, and is associated with a tendency toward more open configurations of the periplasmic binding pocket. In contrast, protonation at Asp645 stabilizes a closed dyad conformation, reduces water accessibility, and narrows the transmembrane binding pocket. These findings support a proposed sequential protonation model in which protonation-dependent conformational changes are allosterically coupled to substrate translocation.</content>

    <title>The successor representation in high-risk drinking and alcohol-related contexts</title>
    <link rel="alternate" href="https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014873" title="The successor representation in high-risk drinking and alcohol-related contexts" />

    <content type="html"><p>by Milena Philomena Maria Musial, Sam Hall-McMaster, Kanji Shimomura, Ayaka Kato, Erik L. Bode, Clarissa C. Grundmann, Claudia Ebrahimi, Kenji Morita, Samuel J. Gershman, Tanja Endrass, Florian Schlagenhauf</p>

The successor representation (SR) is a reinforcement learning strategy which has been suggested to underlie nuanced forms of habitual behavior, rendering it a candidate mechanism for mental health conditions thought to involve habitual control, such as addiction. However, paradigms used to assess habits in humans cannot detect SR use. Together with the fact that they are usually conducted in disorder-irrelevant contexts, this may explain why the evidence for a hypothesized shift from goal-directed to habitual behavior in addiction is inconsistent. Here, we tested whether individuals with high-risk (<i>n</i> = 260) compared to low-risk drinking behavior (<i>n</i> = 260) rely more on SR or a rigid goal-based dimension-reduced SR variant, particularly in alcohol-related contexts. An online multi-stage decision-making task performed in either a virtual bar or apartment context allowed us to dissociate (red)SR from model-based and model-free learning strategies by testing how well participants adapted their choices to different types of distal changes in the environment. Findings suggest that a particular type of SR, namely a (reduced) random-policy SR-like strategy, contributes to human behavior, but that high-risk drinkers do not differ from low-risk drinkers in their use of this strategy. Instead, both groups seem to rely less on what is likely a (reduced) random-policy SR strategy in alcohol-related contexts – and instead more on model-free control. Results suggest that the use of an adaptive, resource-efficient decision-making strategy is selectively downregulated in substance-related contexts. This study highlights the importance of considering contextual modulation and nuanced decision strategies in understanding habitual and goal-directed behavior in mental health conditions such as addiction.</content>

    <content type="html"><p>by Lucy M. Devlin, Phi H. Nguyen, Ross N. Cuthbert, Phu Ngoc Doan, Viet Hung Tran, Zichi Zhang, Archie K. Murchie, Connor G. G. Bamford, Jaimie T. A. Dick, Eric R. Morgan, Thai S. Mai</p>

Reliable early warning of infectious disease outbreaks remains a major challenge for surveillance systems, particularly for vector-borne pathogens whose transmission depends on interactions among hosts, vectors, and climate-sensitive environmental conditions. Data-driven forecasting offers a promising approach for predicting outbreak risk using surveillance and environmental data. This study develops a logit-weighted ensemble (LWE), a machine-learning framework that predicts outbreak occurrence 1–6 months ahead at the administrative unit–month scale using routinely available outbreak notifications and gridded climate data. Bluetongue virus (BTV), an arbovirus of ruminants transmitted by <i>Culicoides</i> biting midges, provides a well-characterised system in which transmission is strongly shaped by climate, making it a useful system for applying and testing this approach. The framework is evaluated using surveillance data collected between 2005 and 2024 from France, Greece, and Italy, selected for their long-running and high-quality outbreak surveillance records. Across all three countries, the LWE achieved the strongest and most stable predictive performance under a recall-focused evaluation that prioritises correctly identifying outbreak months. It outperformed or matched 14 benchmark models, with differences becoming more pronounced at longer lead times (month +3 onward), when predictions are more uncertain and outbreaks are relatively rare. Predictability varied across countries, with the highest performance in Greece, strong performance in France, and lower, more variable performance in Italy, reflecting differences in how consistently outbreaks occur and spread across regions. Overall, the results demonstrate that horizon-aware, climate-informed forecasting can reliably identify months and locations at elevated risk of outbreak occurrence up to six months in advance, supporting surveillance planning and preparedness across heterogeneous European settings. The ensemble framework provides a robust and portable strategy for outbreak prediction using routinely collected surveillance and environmental data.</content>

Motivation <p>Predicting drug sensitivity across diverse cancer samples is a fundamental challenge in personalized therapy and drug discovery. This task requires comprehensive characterization of both drug and cancer cell line features. Current approaches often fail to fully capture the complex structural characteristics and interactions of drug compounds and struggle to integrate multi-omics features derived from the same sample, limiting their feature representation capacity. Consequently, there is a need for modeling frameworks that can jointly model molecular structural features and multi-modal cellular contexts in a unified manner.</p> Results <p>We present SADRP, a structurally aware multi-modal framework for drug response prediction, designed to model complex molecular structures and multi-omics data. For drug representation, SADRP incorporates Shortest Distance Path (SDP) encoding and edge encoding to capture both topological relationships and bond-type chemical semantics. For cell line profiling, a multi-view interactive encoder integrates gene expression and DNA methylation, capturing cross-omics synergistic complementarity. SADRP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, while also identifying potential therapeutic candidates and biomarkers, providing mechanistic insights and supporting applications in drug discovery and personalized medicine.</p></content>

    <content type="html"><p>by Nan Qiu, Fredrik Allenmark, Siyi Chen, Hermann J. Müller, Zhuanghua Shi</p>

Real-world distractors occur in environments whose states change at different rates. We asked whether such volatility alters initial overt oculomotor allocation, later target verification and response commitment, or both. Observers performed an additional-singleton search task with concurrent eye tracking while distractor presence followed high- or low-volatility sequences, with overall distractor prevalence held constant. Trial-pooled oculomotor capture was higher under high volatility, a pattern that appears to indicate altered filtering. Matching the same-location run position removed that difference, with no detectable difference in capture across volatility regimes at matched run position. The pooled capture effect was therefore consistent with a structural consequence of the volatility manipulation, which enriched high-volatility blocks with early-run positions where capture is intrinsically high. The volatility effect itself appeared on distractor-absent trials. Under high volatility, response times were longer, fixations more frequent, final-target dwell longer, and errors fewer, while target-acquisition latency itself was unchanged. Same-location repetition learning showed no detectable difference in slope across regimes. A hierarchical drift-diffusion model (DDM) and a complementary volatility Kalman-filter (VKF) comparison converged in showing that manual responses carried both boundary-related and drift-related structure. With distractor frequency held constant, the per-trial effect of volatility therefore emerged after the first saccade as an increase in response caution rather than in oculomotor capture. This pattern is consistent with precision-weighted adjustment to environmental uncertainty.</content>

    <content type="html"><p>by Alexandre Coudray, Romain Forey, Benjamin Bejar Haro, Filipe Martins, Joana Carlevaro-Fita, Shaoline Sheppard, Sandra Eloise Offner, Gioele La Manno, Guillaume Obozinski, Didier Trono</p>

Analyses routinely conducted in both fundamental research and biomedical studies often report aggregate signals derived from heterogeneous mixtures of cells. These mixtures reflect the intrinsic anatomical and functional complexity of the tissues and organs from which they are derived. Such bulk measurements obscure cell-specific signals, thereby hindering accurate interpretation of the underlying biological processes. Here, we introduce CLIMB and CLIFF, a two-step machine-learning framework that deconvolves bulk RNA-seq into cell-type composition and expression, and then resolves bulk drug sensitivity measurements into cell subtype- and single-cell-specific profiles. We first validate CLIMB using in-vitro mixtures of leukemic cell lines with experimentally known cell-type proportions, then extend this validation to large-scale, cross-dataset pseudo-bulk analyses built from independent scRNA-seq references across two disease contexts and five cancer types — mimicking the reference-to-target mismatches encountered in real applications — and show that CLIMB accurately infers the cellular composition of bulk samples, outperforming state-of-the-art bulk deconvolution methods. We applied our deconvolution strategy to the beatAML cohort dataset, currently the most extensive database of <i>ex-vivo</i> drug screening data. This analysis generated a cell subtype–resolved drug sensitivity landscape for 121 compounds, revealing multiple compounds putatively active against leukemic stem cells, including midostaurin, A-674563, SNS-032, and foretinib.     <content type="html"><p>by Kyle Morrison, Malgorzata Lagisz</p>

In an ideal world, authors would report clearly and transparently exactly what they conducted. In reality, reporting is often incomplete, and key elements of research conduct are frequently missing from manuscripts. Reporting guidelines were developed to address this problem by helping authors identify what should be reported. These guidelines have been highly valuable for authors, but they are not well suited for appraising reporting during peer review or editorial assessment despite common use. This is because authors and appraisers have different needs: authors require a comprehensive guide for writing, whereas appraisers need a tool that is concise, repeatable, and easy to use. We therefore propose the development of reporting appraisal tools: operationalised tools designed specifically to assess whether a paper has reported the minimum essential elements of a study. To support their development, we present 10 simple rules.</content>

    <content type="html"><p>by Frederik De Laender, Andrew Gonzalez, Olivia Bleeckx, Dieter Ebert, György Barabás</p>

We provide a general theoretical explanation for a longstanding result in spatial ecology: weak dispersal among habitat patches promotes local species richness. Using analytical approximations of spatial Lotka–Volterra competition models, we show that local species persistence in heterogeneous landscapes can be expressed as the balance between the total density across patches and the local exclusion rate. We further demonstrate that local multispecies coexistence is governed by the feasibility domain, linking spatial coexistence to a structural property of nonspatial competitive systems. Together, these results explain why weak dispersal increases local species richness and why this effect strengthens with the number of available patches, i.e., landscape size. We test these predictions using numerical simulations and find that the theory breaks down only when both dispersal and competitive interactions are very strong, in which case dispersal has a unimodal effect on coexistence. In contrast, landscape size retains a positive effect on coexistence whenever an effect is detectable. We then apply the theory to long-term data from a natural metacommunity of microcrustaceans. We detect strong competition among species and find no detectable effect of dispersal rate on local coexistence, whereas species co-occurrence increases with local landscape size, as predicted by theory. Together, our results identify how dispersal, interaction strength, and landscape size jointly regulate local species richness in competitive systems.</content>

    <content type="html"><p>by Adhityo Wicaksono, Arli Aditya Parikesit</p>

A constraint-first framework for future ‘prompt-to-genome’ AI across Bacteria, Archaea, Eukaryota, and viruses is proposed. Genome-scale models can now generate long DNA sequences, and experimentally viable genome-scale designs have begun to appear, but sequence generation alone does not establish biological feasibility. Constraints should not require designs to remain within natural sequence space; rather, they should define testable boundaries for function, inheritance, lifecycle coherence and safe use, including new-to-nature designs. We propose a two-part system. First, a Constraint Compiler translates natural-language prompts into machine-checkable specifications defining scope, context, objectives, assumptions and governance requirements. Second, a modular Validator Stack (C1–C6) evaluates candidate designs for sequence integrity, gene and regulatory plausibility, genome completeness, comparative coherence, systems-level feasibility, and safety and governance. Extreme prompts serve as stress tests to expose hidden assumptions, conflicting objectives, and refusal points, complemented by adversarial testing and risk assessment. A phased roadmap and community benchmarks are proposed to measure specification accuracy, biological feasibility, robustness, and governance performance. The goal is to move prompt-to-genome systems from impressive generation toward reliable, auditable, and accountable biological design.</content>

Progress in malaria control has stagnated since the early 21st century in many countries, requiring new approaches such as the use of spatially-targeted interventions. However, evidence on the effectiveness of spatially-targeted interventions is mixed, depending on both the setting and intervention. In addition, the potential role of community health programs in implementing spatial targeting is underexplored, with models focusing on coarser spatial scales than those needed to guide programmatic activities. We developed a two-age-class, spatially-explicit model of malaria at the community-scale for a district in southeastern Madagascar, accounting for environmental heterogeneity and spatial structure, to explore spatially-targeted community health interventions. The model was fit to field-based case notifications and malaria prevalence data and then used to simulate three interventions: indoor residual spraying (IRS), supplemental coverage of long-lasting insecticide-treated nets (LLIN), and active case detection (ACD). We compared five scenarios, one with no spatial targeting and others targeting communities (i) nearest to clinics, (ii) furthest from clinics, (iii) with highest incidence, and (iv) that are spatially central. The non-targeted intervention was generally the most effective, but the least resource efficient. The second most effective intervention was based on spatial centrality, which reached a larger population while using fewer transportation resources than the non-targeted intervention. No combination of interventions was able to eliminate malaria in the district, although detecting symptomatic cases through ACD could avert 100% of severe malaria cases at high detection rates. These results highlight the potential for targeted malaria interventions, especially in low-income settings, that take into account spatial structure in the human population and transport networks to reduce malaria burdens using fewer resources than conventional district-wide interventions. A primary goal of systems neuroscience is to discover how ensembles of neurons transform inputs into goal-directed behavior, a process known as neural computation. A powerful framework for understanding neural computation uses neural dynamics – the rules that govern how neural activity evolves over time – to explain how goal-directed input-output transformations occur. As dynamical rules are not directly observable, we need computational models that can infer neural dynamics from recorded neural activity. We typically validate such models using synthetic datasets with known ground-truth dynamics, but unfortunately existing synthetic datasets don’t reflect fundamental features of neural computation and may therefore be poor proxies for neural systems. Further, the field lacks validated metrics for quantifying the accuracy of the dynamics inferred by models. The Computation-through-Dynamics Toolkit (CtDToolkit) addresses these critical gaps by providing: 1) synthetic datasets that reflect computational properties of biological neural circuits, 2) interpretable metrics for quantifying model performance, and 3) a standardized pipeline for training and evaluating models with or without known external inputs. In this manuscript, we demonstrate how CtDToolkit can help guide the development, tuning, and troubleshooting of neural dynamics models. In summary, CtDToolkit provides a necessary framework for model developers to better understand and characterize neural computation through the lens of dynamics.</content>

The adaptive immune system recognizes billions of unique antigens using highly variable T cell receptors (TCRs). To what extent TCR features shape the spatial distribution of the TCR repertoire (TCR-R) within lymphoid organs remains unclear. Here, we compared the TCR-R composition in T cell zones (TCZ), B cell zones (BCZ), and germinal centers (GC) of the spleen by analyzing the complementarity-determining region 3 of the beta chain (CDR3β) in microdissected splenic compartments from naïve and immunized mice. After immunization, expanded clones started appearing in the TCZ at day 3 and later shifted to the BCZ. Similarly, while TCR length and closeness to germline initially showed more pronounced differences between the compartments, our models of random distribution and proliferation explained these differences almost entirely. This would imply that quantitative assessment of TCR-R dynamics across heterogeneous spatial compartments during an immune response is only possible when these effects are explicitly accounted for.</content>

    <content type="html"><p>by Li Zhou, Yun Zuo, Wenying He, Zhaohong Deng</p>

Drug-drug interactions (DDIs) are critical in pharmacology, as synergistic or antagonistic effects between co-administered drugs can enhance therapeutic outcomes or cause toxicity, posing major challenges for drug safety assessment and new drug development. Current molecular representation methods often fail to capture dynamic substructure relationships or semantic interactions among functional groups. To overcome these limitations, this study proposes MEGH-DDI, a multimodal framework that integrates complementary molecular representation learning with graph-structure dynamic perception. The framework employs a dual-channel semantic module that combines Mol2vec-based substructure representations with MolT5 chemical language embeddings, while SHAP-based dynamic feature selection reduces redundancy. For fine-grained structural modeling, we introduce an edge-aware GCNII equipped with bond-level attention to distinguish different types of chemical bonds. Furthermore, the Hop2Token module converts multi-hop neighborhoods into token sequences, enabling Transformer-based modeling of high-order substructure dependencies. Experimental results demonstrate that MEGH-DDI achieves competitive performance across both transductive and inductive settings. On the DrugBank dataset, MEGH-DDI attains an accuracy of 98.36% in the transductive task, outperforming earlier baselines and surpassing recent state-of-the-art methods, with both AUC and AP exceeding 99.7%. On the ChChMiner dataset, MEGH-DDI achieves an F1 score of 99.05%, improving over the best existing method by 2.74 percentage points. In the inductive settings, MEGH-DDI achieves competitive performance across most evaluation metrics on both datasets, showing advantages over competing methods on several key metrics. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of MEGH-DDI in predicting DDI involving previously unseen drugs and its potential to generalize to complex DDI prediction scenarios. To enhance interpretability, MEGH-DDI incorporates a three-level mechanism spanning atoms, chemical bonds, and topological paths, highlighting key atoms and bond contributions. Overall, MEGH-DDI provides an efficient, accurate, and interpretable solution for drug safety assessment and new drug discovery. Glycoprotein VI (GPVI) and C-type lectin-like receptor 2 (CLEC-2) are platelet-activating receptors whose extracellular organization contributes to receptor association and signaling during thrombus formation, yet how alternative receptor architectures influence mechanical persistence remains unclear. These results show that alternative extracellular arrangements of the same receptor are not mechanically equivalent and that uncertainty in GPVI architecture can translate into large differences in force transmission and persistence under load.     <content type="html"><p>by Ing Xhu Lim, Faisal Halabeya, Joshua N. Milstein</p>

Understanding how structures arise in microbial communities remains an outstanding challenge in bacterial ecology. When replicating within dense and confined environments, bacterial populations may collectively self-organize as a result of mechanical interactions. We previously observed that model dual-populations of bacteria, colonizing open-ended microchannels, either quickly fixate to a single population or segregate into long-lived, coexisting populations. This latter quasi-stability results from the alignment of bacteria into lanes, forcing cells to grow toward the open ends of the channel, with inter-lane invasion events driving the boundary dynamics between populations. Here we apply agent-based (AB) simulations to explore the boundary dynamics between dual-bacterial populations of varying morphology and division rate. We find that the simulated boundary dynamics are well-described by a simple drift-diffusion model, which enables us to estimate the mean time to fixation within competitive scenarios where the fixation time is difficult to access by AB simulations. Coccus-like cells display a competitive advantage over bacillus cells as they can more effectively invade and ultimately fixate, while coexisting populations of bacillus cells are “effectively” stable. And while faster-dividing cells should have a selective advantage, their morphology determines if this advantage drives fixation or acts as a defensive strategy to maintain their population. These findings highlight the critical role that cell morphology and mechanics play in shaping bacterial communities.</content>

Identifying cancer driver genes and their therapeutic impact remains a core challenge in computational cancer biology. We introduce xNNDriver and xAEDriver, two interpretable neural network frameworks that connect cancer mutations with genome-wide DepMap gene dependencies, pathway activity, and drug-response patterns. xNNDriver is a supervised pathway-guided model that evaluates whether a gene’s mutation status is encoded in the genome-wide dependency landscape; we interpret model fitness as a driver potential score, which quantifies the strength of this mutation-dependency signal and prioritizes genes with broad functional footprints. Across 3,008 candidate genes, xNNDriver recovers major established drivers and highlights literature-supported candidates, while pathway analyses reveal biologically coherent programs related to metabolism, growth factor signaling, and immune regulation. To capture combinatorial functional states, xAEDriver uses an unsupervised autoencoder to learn Driver Variant Representations (DVRs), latent binary features guided by the frequency distribution of known driver mutations. DVRs capture cell-line-specific dependency patterns and expression patterns and are associated with drug sensitivity and pathway activity. Together, these interpretable deep learning models demonstrate that gene dependency landscapes encode rich, interpretable signals of oncogenic function and provide a hypothesis-generating framework for prioritizing drivers, pathways, and therapeutic vulnerabilities for further experimental validation.</content>

NK cells express a wide array of inhibitory and activating receptors on the cell surface including the activating receptor NKG2D. Receptor signaling in NK cells leads to rapid post-translational modification (e.g., phosphorylation) of sub-cellular signaling proteins within minutes of receptor stimulation that ultimately give rise to diverse effector functions including cell proliferation. Ecologists and conservation biologists rely on genetic diversity as a key essential biodiversity variable (EBV) used to track population health and dynamics, and utilize the population-scaled mutation parameter θ as a key metric of diversity. While whole-genome-sequencing (wgs) is increasingly affordable, it will be considerable time before the full diversity of life is represented by high-quality assembled genomes; even then, constant monitoring will still require repeated sampling across time and space. In contrast, genome skimming (low-coverage, short-read wgs) is highly cost-effective but challenging to analyze because the coverage is too low for assembly and reliable error correction. Mature methods, such as Mash, exist for estimating pairwise genomic distances based on the Jaccard similarity of <i>k</i>-mer sets computed using sketching techniques. Some, such as Skmer, additionally model the impacts of low coverage. These methods have been successfully applied to assembly-free species identification and phylogenetics; however, their use in population genetics has been limited. Among other limitations, these methods implicitly treat genomes as haploid, and heterozygosity confounds estimates of genomic distance for diploid organisms. In this paper, we address this problem through several technical advances. First, we use coalescent theory to mathematically derive how the Jaccard index between the k-mer sets of two diploid samples changes with θ under a neutral Kingman’s coalescent model. Next, we model the impact of coverage and sequencing error to derive an estimate of θ from the Jaccard index, in addition to several auxiliary variables, which we also estimate from the genome skims. The resulting method, DipSkmer, enables more accurate estimates of coverage, sequencing error, and θ for diploid samples. Analyses of both simulated and empirical datasets show that for diploids and low distances (e.g., < 2%), DipSkmer’s estimate outperforms existing alignment-free methods such as Mash and Skmer, and closely approximates ANGSD, a reference and alignment-based tool.</content>

Forecasting emerging infectious disease outbreaks is particularly challenging for sexual networks of men who have sex with men (MSM), where transmission can be shaped by heterogeneous and overdispersed contact structures, mixing assortativity, and both one-time and recurrent partnerships. Our findings suggest a practical approach for robust forecasting in highly overdispersed networks, where distinguishing network effects from other factors remains challenging and usually requires additional data.</content>

Phase mapping is a widespread method for identifying rotational electrical activity sustaining cardiac arrhythmias. However, conventional implementations assume that the cardiac phase map is continuous, leading to ill-defined phase indices in regions affected by functional conduction block, fibrosis, or anatomical boundaries. These regions of discontinuous or undefined phase, termed phase defects, lead to both false positive and false negative detections of rotational drivers. This work introduces an improved phase mapping implementation termed <i>extended phase mapping</i> that explicitly detects and accounts for phase defects, enabling robust calculation of the phase index around them. Extended phase mapping is applied to (1) simulated excitation patterns using the Fenton–Karma model, (2) experimental optical mapping data of rat ventricular fibrillation, and (3) a clinical CARTO activation map of atrial tachycardia. Across all datasets, the extended approach eliminates erroneous detections and resolves previously missed rotations. Our results demonstrate that proper treatment of phase defects yields a unified and physiologically consistent characterization of all rotational drivers including near-complete and anatomical reentries. Therefore, we propose that explicitly accounting for phase defects, rather than tracking singular points alone, gives a more complete and consistent characterization of rotational dynamics in cardiac tissue.</content>
